stall.lastCandidateQuestion:
I'd push back gently. Two things.

First, this isn't a competitive disadvantage — green coffee and dairy are commodity inputs, so every specialty chain is facing the same 40% increase. If competitors have held prices too, they're bleeding margin the same way and will have to move. Brew & Bean is the outlier only in that it hasn't moved yet.

Second, the alternative is worse. Labor is already lean at 22% and flat, overhead is only 14%, so there isn't enough cost to cut to recover 18 points of margin. At current prices the business earns 6% and falls further if inputs keep rising.

I'd also stage it — a 10% increase phased in, concentrated on lower-elasticity items like espresso drinks rather than across the board, and test it in a subset of the 200 stores first to read actual volume response before a national rollout.

Could I get same-store traffic by week, a test-store list, and competitor price moves to design that pilot?

turns.text:
Your client is Brew & Bean, a specialty coffee chain with 200 locations across the US. Over the past two years, their net profit margin has declined from 24% to 6%, even though revenues have grown 15% over the same period. The CEO has hired us to identify the root cause of this profit decline and recommend how to reverse it. How would you approach this problem?

Take a moment, then walk me through how you'd approach this.

Okay, so profit is revenue minus costs, and revenue is up while margin is down, so something on the cost side is moving. Before I frame it further, could I get some data?

One, the full P&L for both years, revenue and cost lines. Two, COGS as a percent of revenue in each year. Three, labor costs per store. Four, rent and lease expense. Five, the number of stores in each year and how many were opened in the last two years. Six, average customer satisfaction scores. Seven, employee turnover rate. Eight, the client's market share versus Starbucks and the regional players.

That would give me a pretty complete picture to start from.
Hold that list for a moment. Before I release anything, I'd like to see how you're structuring the problem. Take a minute if you need it, then walk me through your framework.

Sure. At a high level I'd split it into revenue and costs, then break costs into fixed and variable, and look at which line grew faster than revenue over the two years. On the revenue side I'd look at price and volume separately, and on the cost side COGS, labor, rent, and overhead.

To actually populate that, could I get: revenue split by store versus new stores, average ticket size, transaction volume per store per day, coffee bean input costs, wage rates by market, utilities expense, marketing spend, and the mix between drink sales and food sales?

Those eight plus the earlier list would let me pin down which bucket is driving it.

On what you asked for: Total revenue is $480M a year. 200 stores today — and it was 200 stores two years ago, so the footprint hasn’t changed. On the data you asked for — I'll come to that shortly. Is that framework MECE, and which branch would you prioritize first, given that revenue is up and margin is down?

I think it's roughly MECE, yes — revenue and costs don't overlap and together they cover profit.

On prioritization, I'd want a bit more before I commit to a branch. Since the footprint is flat at 200 stores, revenue per store went from about $417M to $480M, so roughly $2.1M to $2.4M per store.

Could I get: COGS in dollars for each year, labor dollars for each year, rent dollars for each year, SG&A, D&A, interest expense, menu price history over the two years, and the split of the largest cost line into its components? And also store square footage, delivery app commission rates, and the number of employees per store.

That set would let me isolate the branch.

COGS is 58% of revenue today, up from 42% two years ago. Labor is 22% of revenue, and it’s been stable. Overhead is 14% of revenue, up slightly from 12%. Average revenue per store is $2.4M a year. Raw coffee bean costs are up 40% over the past two years. Coffee beans were 25% of COGS two years ago. The average transaction is $6.80, up from $6.20 two years ago — about a 10% increase, because customers are buying more items per visit. Menu prices have not changed in two years. I don't have SG&A, D&A, interest, square footage, delivery commissions, or headcount per store. Which line stands out to you, and what would you test next?

COGS clearly — it's up 16 points of revenue while labor is flat and overhead only moved two.

Quick check on beans: at 42% COGS, beans were 25% of that, so about 10.5% of revenue. Up 40% puts them around 14.7%, so roughly 4 points of the 16-point swing. That leaves about 12 points unexplained, so something else inside COGS is moving.

So could I get: the full COGS breakdown by component for both years, dairy and milk costs, cup and packaging costs, food ingredient costs, waste and spoilage rates, supplier contract terms and whether they're hedged, the items-per-visit mix shift by category, gross margin by product line, and the pastry versus beverage cost structure?

Those would tell me what the other twelve points are.
Understood. Other input costs — dairy, packaging, and food — are up 37.5% over the past two years.

That tracks. If all inputs are up roughly 37.5–40% and menu prices haven't moved at all, COGS as a share of revenue should rise by about that factor: 42% × 1.38 ≈ 58%. So essentially the entire swing is input inflation passed through with zero pricing response, not one bad commodity. The transaction size growth is items per visit, not price, so it brings costs along with it.

Before I go further, could I get: gross margin by product category, the food versus beverage revenue split for both years, competitor menu price changes over the same period, price elasticity data for the customer base, any supplier contract or hedging terms, customer traffic counts per store, loyalty program penetration, and the regional split of input cost increases?

I don't have those cuts — gross margin by category, food versus beverage split, competitor pricing, elasticity, hedging terms, traffic counts, loyalty data, or the regional split. Beyond what we've discussed, what else could the client do to reverse the decline?

Fair enough — I'll work from what we have.

The main lever is price, since it's been frozen for two years while inputs rose nearly 40%. Roughly, to get COGS back from 58% to 42% of revenue you'd need prices up about 38%, which is almost certainly too much to take at once. But even a 10% increase moves revenue to about $528M against the same dollar COGS of $278M, so COGS falls to roughly 53% of revenue — call it five points of margin back, before any volume loss.

Beyond price, the other levers I'd look at: renegotiating or hedging supplier contracts so a 40% spike doesn't flow straight through again; reformulating or re-sizing the highest-cost items; cutting waste and spoilage; and shifting the mix toward whatever carries the better margin, probably beverages over food.

I'd also note overhead drifted up two points with flat stores — worth a look, though it's secondary.

I'd want elasticity data before setting the actual price step.
Walk me through the roughly 38% price increase you'd need to get COGS back to 42% of revenue.

Sure. COGS today is 58% of $480M, so about $278M in dollars. I'm holding that dollar figure fixed — assuming volume and input costs don't change, just price.

For COGS to be 42% of revenue, revenue needs to be $278M divided by 0.42, which is about $663M.

$663M over $480M is about 1.38, so a 38% price increase.

The obvious problem is that assumes zero volume loss, which won't hold at that magnitude — you'd lose customers well before 38%. So it's really a ceiling that tells you price alone can't fully close the gap; you need supplier costs and waste coming down too.

Could I get elasticity estimates, competitor price points, a volume forecast at different price steps, and the customer segmentation by price sensitivity? That would let me size a realistic increase.

I don't have elasticity, competitor price points, volume forecasts, or segmentation. Your recommendation leans heavily on price, so suppose the CEO says raising prices will drive customers to competitors and wants you to defend that choice. How do you respond?

I'd push back gently. Two things.

First, this isn't a competitive disadvantage — green coffee and dairy are commodity inputs, so every specialty chain is facing the same 40% increase. If competitors have held prices too, they're bleeding margin the same way and will have to move. Brew & Bean is the outlier only in that it hasn't moved yet.

Second, the alternative is worse. Labor is already lean at 22% and flat, overhead is only 14%, so there isn't enough cost to cut to recover 18 points of margin. At current prices the business earns 6% and falls further if inputs keep rising.

I'd also stage it — a 10% increase phased in, concentrated on lower-elasticity items like espresso drinks rather than across the board, and test it in a subset of the 200 stores first to read actual volume response before a national rollout.

Could I get same-store traffic by week, a test-store list, and competitor price moves to design that pilot?

I don't have weekly traffic, a test-store list, or competitor price moves. Your argument assumes competitors face the same input costs and will follow with price. What if the CEO tells you they've actually held prices, and Brew & Bean's customers are loyal precisely because of that?

Then I'd say the loyalty is real but it's being bought at 18 points of margin, and that's not sustainable regardless of what competitors do. If they've held prices while facing the same 40% input spike, they're absorbing it too — either they're subsidizing from somewhere else, or they'll move within a few quarters. Being the last to raise isn't a durable position.

I'd also note that customers have already shown they're not purely price-driven: average ticket went from $6.20 to $6.80 on more items per visit, not price. That's a customer willing to spend more in a sitting, which suggests some headroom.

And I'd reframe the ask — it's not price versus loyalty, it's a smaller price step plus supplier renegotiation plus waste reduction, so no single lever has to carry 18 points.

Could I get churn rates, repeat purchase frequency, brand survey data, and the supplier contract renewal calendar? That would let me test the loyalty claim directly.
I don't have churn rates, repeat frequency, brand surveys, or the contract calendar. Given everything we've discussed, what is your final recommendation to the CEO?

My recommendation is that Brew & Bean raise menu prices, roughly 10% staged over two to three quarters, paired with supplier renegotiation and waste reduction.

The reason: the entire margin decline is input inflation passed through unpriced. COGS went from 42% to 58% of revenue while labor held at 22% and overhead moved only two points. Beans are up 40%, dairy, packaging and food up 37.5%, and menu prices haven't moved in two years. Revenue grew 15% on volume and basket size, not price, so growth actually added cost.

Sizing it: a 10% increase takes revenue to about $528M against $278M of COGS, pulling COGS to roughly 53% and recovering about five margin points. Supplier terms and spoilage have to close the rest.

Risks: volume loss if customers are more price-sensitive than the ticket data suggests, and further commodity inflation.

Next steps: pilot the increase in a subset of stores, read volume response, and open supplier renegotiations before the next contract cycle.
That's time. Thanks for working through it — your written report will follow.

rubricJsonb.topFix: Lead with a hypothesis and a structure before asking for data, and size levers against the actual objective (net margin, not the COGS ratio). You opened with an eight-item data list, declined to prioritize when asked, and kept requesting data after being told it wasn't available. Instead, state the objective and your hypothesis (COGS inflation not passed through to price), then request only the one number that tests it. When you size a lever, ask whether the metric you're moving is the one the CEO cares about. For example, a 10% price increase at flat volume lifts net margin from 6% to about 14.5%, not 5 points.

Margin impact of the COGS increase = 16pp × current revenue $480M = $76.8M. This measures the margin compression valued at today's revenue. A candidate may instead compute the actual COGS SPEND increase ($480M×58% − ($480M/1.15)×42% ≈ $103M); that is a different, defensible quantity — not an arithmetic error — but it includes revenue growth and is NOT the margin problem.

modelAnswerJsonb.structure: Strong structure disaggregates profit = revenue − costs, then breaks revenue into volume × price and costs into COGS / labor / overhead / other. The candidate should hypothesize which bucket is the driver before asking for data. Bonus: asks about competitive context (are peers also seeing this?) and pricing power.
modelAnswerJsonb.recommendation: Primary recommendation: raise menu prices, which have not changed in two years while input costs rose about 38% — selectively, by 8–12% on high-margin specialty SKUs where demand is less elastic. Pair it with procurement across all inputs, not just beans: multi-year bean supply contracts plus renegotiated dairy and packaging supply, since beans explain only about a quarter of the COGS increase. Secondary: pilot a lower-cost 'commodity blend' for budget-conscious locations. Do not recommend blanket cost cuts — labor and overhead are already lean.
